because he relies on various response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), he mostly transforms the śrāvakas through these.
One should know how many kinds of Buddha-dharmas are subsumed within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
First is the "Pure" [body], because it is attained by transforming the *ālayavijñāna* into the Dharma-body;
second is the "Retribution" [body], because it is attained by transforming the material sense-faculties into the wisdom of retribution.
Regarding "practice," it is the transformation of practice in order to attain the practice of immeasurable wisdom;
regarding "mastery," it is the transformation of the mastery encompassed by various karmas, in order to attain the mastery of unimpeded supernormal knowledge and wisdom in all worlds;

regarding "provisional application," it is the transformation of all seeing, hearing, understanding, and knowing from provisional names, in order to attain the mastery of teaching through wisdom that delights all sentient beings.
"Dispelling" refers to the turning away of all calamities; it means dispelling all the calamities of all sentient beings through the wisdom of dispelling.
One should know that because these are the six kinds of Buddha-dharmas, they are subsumed within the Dharma-body of the Buddhas.
Regarding all these Buddha-dharmakāyas, are they distinct or non-distinct?
They are not distinct because of the differences in body, mind, and activity; yet they are distinct because they manifest perfect enlightenment in immeasurable locations.

As it is with the Dharma-body, so it is with the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*); they are not intermingled because of the distinctions in mental activity, yet there is no distinction in the bodies themselves, as they manifest in immeasurable forms.
The Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) should also be understood in the same manner as the Reward-body.
How many kinds of merits should be known as being possessed by the Dharma-body? They are: the four kinds of pure and stainless immeasurables;

the liberations; the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); the state of purity (*śubhakṛtsna*); the absence of strife (*araṇā*); the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*); the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the four kinds of purity in all aspects; the ten powers (*bala*); the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); the three ways in which there is nothing to guard against (*trīṇy arakṣyāṇi*); the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the destruction of latent tendencies (*vāsanāsamudghāta*); the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharman*); great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); and the wisdom that is fully endowed with all aspects. Thus should it be understood.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
Compassionate toward all sentient beings, With minds that accord with their welfare and hearts that do not seek their disadvantage, To those who bring benefit, I pay homage.
Having attained liberation from all obscurations, the Muni has transcended the world;
his wisdom pervades all that is knowable. I take refuge in him whose mind is liberated.
Among all beings without exception, he has extinguished every affliction.
Unmixed, he extinguishes the afflictions; I take refuge in him who dwells in the heights.
Spontaneously free from all obstructions, never regressing, he constantly enters meditative absorption.
Amidst all manner of hardships, I take refuge in the one who can deliver us.
Regarding the body and its basis, speech and wisdom, and the speaker—your mind never falters; I take refuge in you, the excellent teacher.
You know their speech from afar, and you know the minds of others as they come and go.
Within the unreality of sentient beings, you take refuge in excellent instruction;
you praise the adoption of the Dharma of the Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). All living beings behold the Sage;
having beheld him, they immediately give rise to reverence. I take refuge in the one who discerns.
In the spheres of perception and all powers, Within the emanation bodies and vows,
With mastery over samādhi and wisdom, I take refuge in those who have reached the further shore.
Through skillful means, they take refuge in purity, Bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
The Mahāyāna’s supramundane benefit, I take refuge in the one who subdues Māra.
Through wisdom he extinguishes [suffering] and brings about transcendence; he creates obstacles and provides exposition.
Regarding self, others, and non-Buddhists, I take refuge in the one who is irreversible.
The Great Assembly is skilled in teaching, Free from the two kinds of defilement;
Without need for protection, yet never to be forgotten— I take refuge in the One who leads the assembly.
In the practice of all conduct, There is nothing the Noble One does not know.
Knowing all things at all times, I take refuge in the one whose meaning is reality.
Amidst the deeds of sentient beings, the Noble One’s vision is never at variance;
his activities never cease for a moment—I take refuge in the one who is not false.
Throughout one day and one night, you observe sentient beings during the six periods;
having perfected great compassion, I take refuge in you whose mind brings benefit.
Whether in action, attainment, wisdom, or all karmic deeds, [I take refuge in you].
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas take refuge in the Supreme One.
The Great Bodhi of the three bodies, possessing all marks,
Pervading everywhere among all beings— I take refuge in the one who resolves all doubts.

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas accomplishes such virtues as these; furthermore, there are other natures, causes, fruits, functions, conforming practices, and merits. Therefore, it should be understood that the Dharma-body of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, is called the "unsurpassed merit."
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
Having accomplished all realities, Transcending all stages,
Reaching the pinnacle above all beings, He delivers and liberates all beings.
Possessing immeasurable and boundless merit visible to the world,
yet invisible to all humans and devas within the world; nevertheless,
it is profound, most profound— how can that profound matter of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas be known?
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
The birthless gives birth to all Buddhas; Abiding nowhere, they are well-abiding.
All things are spontaneous; Food consists of four kinds of nutriment.
Non-destruction and the immeasurable, the immeasurable and the single karma, non-perception and the perception of karma—thus are the three bodies of the Buddhas accomplished.
There is no one who attains perfect enlightenment; it is not that all are not Buddhas.
Moment-to-moment, it is immeasurable; It is manifested through both phenomena and non-phenomena.
Whether unstained or stained, And including that which stains and its basis— When neither stained nor unstained, One enters the true essence of reality.
The Buddhas have transcended all aggregates (skandha) and abide within the true aggregate;
they are neither other than it nor identical to it. Having relinquished that, they attain the excellence of cessation.
All things are a mixture of karma; only by leaving the waters of the great ocean can one be free.
Having finished one task, he begins another; he has no thought for his own benefit.
He perceives no faults in sentient beings; like the moon in a shattered vessel, that light of Dharma pervades all worlds like the sun.
Sometimes they attain perfect enlightenment, and sometimes they enter nirvāṇa like a fire;
yet there is no time when they are absent, for the bodies of all Buddhas are eternally abiding.
It is not that the Buddhas lack the True Dharma, nor do people fail to proceed toward the evil realms.
Within the dharmas that are not the holy life, one practices within the locus of the true body.
That practice occurs in all places as well as in no place;
seeing within every body, there is no objective realm for any of the sense faculties.
To eliminate all afflictions is like using a mantra to neutralize toxic medicine;
when afflictions reach their end, one attains the omniscience of all Buddhas.
When afflictions reach the state of the Path, that is the world’s state of quiescent extinction.
Therefore, the great skillful means of all Buddhas are inconceivable. Furthermore, this profound depth should be understood to consist of twelve kinds:

namely, the profundity of the activity of generation and maintenance; the profundity of the activity of differentiation and calculation; the profundity of attaining perfect enlightenment; the profundity of wearying detachment; the profundity of extinguishing the aggregates (*skandha*); the profundity of teaching and transforming; the profundity of manifesting at the [proper] time; the profundity of manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment and entering *nirvāṇa*; the profundity of practice; the profundity of manifesting one's own body; the profundity of extinguishing afflictions (*kleśa*); and the profundity of the meaning of the *dharmakāya*, which is inconceivable.
When bodhisattvas bring the Buddhas to mind, what is the nature of their mindfulness and what is the object of that mindfulness?
Briefly stated, bodhisattvas bring the Buddhas to mind by means of seven aspects.
Because all Buddhas have attained mastery over time and phenomena, they cultivate mindfulness of the Buddhas to attain unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout all worlds.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
"Within the obstacles, the causes are deficient; They pervade the realm of sentient beings.
The Buddhas lack mastery over them, For they are fixed as two types of conformities."
The eternal body of all Tathāgatas exists because suchness is eternally liberated from defilements.
The most subtle evil of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas has been utterly removed because they are free from all afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions.
The Buddhas are spontaneous because they spontaneously perform all Buddha-activities without rest.
The Buddhas possess great power because they experience the joy of great power within the purity of the Buddha-worlds.
The Buddhas are unstained because, though born into the world, all worldly dharmas cannot defile them.

The great purpose of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment and nirvāṇa, so as to transform those sentient beings not yet transformed and to bring liberation to those already transformed.
A verse is spoken therein:
It exists solely within one's own mind, Constantly manifested through power and purity;
Not something produced by effort, it is the Great Dharma, Attained through the body of retribution.
Acting without haste, manifesting again in many births—
the wise should remember all these Buddhas. Furthermore, what is the nature of the purification of the Buddha-worlds?
As it is said in the introductory section of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in one hundred thousand verses:

"The Tathāgata is adorned with the most radiant seven jewels; he emits great light throughout immeasurable worlds because he dwells in the midst of immeasurable, well-discriminated abodes. He transcends the realm of differentiated spheres and the domain of the three realms; he is the locus of the marks of pure, sovereign consciousness, born from supramundane and supreme roots of goodness."

It is the place empowered by the Tathāgata, the dwelling place of great Bodhisattvas, the realm frequented by immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; it is the place moistened by the delight in the flavor of the Great Dharma, the place where all sentient beings appear and perform all manner of deeds, the place free from the affliction of all defilements, and the place free from all Māras; it is the place of the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s adornment that transcends all other adornments, the place reached through the power of great mindfulness and intention, the place of the vehicle of great śamatha and vipaśyanā, the place of entry into the great emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and the place where one dwells within a great and wondrous hall adorned with great lotus kings for immeasurable kalpas.

This is the clarity, color, worldly appearance, magnitude, and power of this Buddha-world’s purity; the power of the place of giving, the cause of giving, and the fruit of giving; the powers of all phenomena, the power of companions, the power of retinues, the power of benefits, the power of karmic activity, the power of moisture, the power of fearlessness, the power of dwelling places, the power of conduct, the power of vehicles, the power of support, the power of gateways, and the power of the expositions of the teachings.
However, within the purity of that Buddha-world, the appearance and power of its forms are exclusively pure, exclusively blissful, exclusively non-evil, and exclusively sovereign.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the Buddha-dharmadhātu performs five kinds of activities at all times:
it protects sentient beings from various calamities, and because those who behold it are freed from such calamities as deafness, blindness, muteness, and insanity.
The activity of rescuing and protecting from the various evil realms consists of exhorting those in unwholesome states to abide in wholesome states.

The activity of preventing obstacles through skillful means consists of causing those among the various non-Buddhists who practice liberation without skillful means to abandon them and abide in the Buddha-dharma.
Because one shares the same views as one's kin, one guards against difficulties in performing deeds; because one transcends the three realms, one assists in the practice of the Path.

By guarding against difficulties in performing deeds, one causes those bodhisattvas who abide in other vehicles, as well as those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage, to practice and abide in the Mahāyāna.
Among these five kinds of activities, one should know that they constitute the activities of all Buddhas and the like.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"Because of the distinctions in the activities performed by the body, And because of the explanation of the various distinctions among conditioned phenomena,"
Because he possesses superior power, he exists for all the worlds; it is not because he is non-existent that the Tathāgatas exist.

If this unique [nature], which is not shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, achieves such merit and power through the Dharmakāya common to all Buddhas, with what intention was it taught as the One Vehicle?
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
Because they grasp at a remainder separately, And because they maintain a remainder,
This is taught for those who are not yet settled, As the principle of the Single Vehicle of all Buddhas.
Believing in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), yet acknowledging the distinctions between their natures,
and because of the profound mind’s response to those to be transformed, the ultimate limit is but the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
For what reason do all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, being identical in their Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), nevertheless speak of many Buddha-activities?
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
In a single realm there are no two [Buddhas], For their constant activities are identical;
Because successive actions would not be sequential, The manifold deeds of the Buddhas are thus established.
Why do the Buddhas of the Dharmakāya not enter final nirvāṇa?
It should be understood that it is not the case that they do not enter final nirvāṇa.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
Far removed from all obscurations, yet with their activities never-ending,
the Buddhas have eternally entered cessation, yet even this is not called "cessation.
For what reason is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) not said to be fully endowed with the *dharmakāya* (truth body)?
Because there are six aspects: because he manifests the form-body (rūpakāya);
because he appears distinctly within immeasurable Buddha-worlds;
and because he appears in accordance with faith.
Because it does not definitively perceive reality, as it appears through various divergent views;
because it manifests common worldly affairs through the diverse and mixed perceptions of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and others;
and because it manifests through the transformation of the ālayavijñāna and so forth—it constitutes only the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) and is not called the true body (*dharmakāya*).
For what reason is it that this is called only the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and not the *dharmakāya* (true body)?
It is because it possesses the eight marks.
When the bodhisattvas attain the *asaṃhārya-samādhi* (unshakable samādhi) at a distant time, the events of being born among the Tuṣita devas or among human beings would not be accomplished.

One who possesses knowledge of past lives does not fail to understand writing, arithmetic, calculation, seals, and treatises on the arts and crafts; nor does he fail to know how to engage in the pursuit of sensual desires and other such activities.
Having understood both the poorly taught and the well-taught doctrines, he does not fail to approach and attend upon the dwellings of non-Buddhist practitioners.
Because he thoroughly understands the practices of the three vehicles, his ascetic practices do not constitute [true] suffering.
He abandoned ten billion Jambudvīpas; yet within a single Jambudvīpa, he attained perfect enlightenment, whereas turning the wheel of Dharma was not accomplished [in the others].

While manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment in the intermediate state as a skillful means, he performs buddha-activities through other emanation bodies in various places; yet, since he attains perfect enlightenment only within Tuṣita Heaven, for what reason does he not simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment throughout all of Jambudvīpa?
In this knowledge, there is no scriptural authority (*āgama*) to be found, nor is there any further meaning that can be established through interpretation.

Furthermore, it is because it would be contradictory for two Buddhas to appear simultaneously in a single world-system; because [a Buddha] manifests many emanations (*nirmāṇa*) to encompass the worlds of the four directions; and because it is as [impossible] as two Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) being born at the same time.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
Because all Buddhas have not yet manifested their transformations, They collectively arrive at the treasury of many [qualities].
All characteristics are realized as awakening; Seeing them, they are able to practice accordingly.

The task of benefiting all sentient beings and the cultivation of the ten thousand practices for the sake of great enlightenment would never enter into nirvana if one did not fulfill these vows and practices; for to cultivate them in vain would yield no fruit.
Since the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are impermanent, how can the Buddhas possess an eternal body?
It is because they rely upon the eternal Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); whereas for all causal bodies, response bodies, and reward bodies, there is no fixed permanence.

Furthermore, regarding the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), one should understand that its constant activities consist in manifesting meritorious qualities as if constantly experiencing bliss and as if constantly possessing power.
Although the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless, in the sphere of the Buddhas' meaning, there is no engagement in activities through artificial contrivance.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
The virtues of all Buddhas are supreme, without distinction, and immeasurable; If sentient beings were weak in their causes, those [virtues] would not be attained;
Having attained them, they are entirely without cause; Were there cessation, they could not be established in accordance with reality.
